It measures the underlying or persistent trend in consumer price dynamics, filtering out transitory price movements. The specific exclusions, weighting methodology, and construction approach vary across countries and are defined by the national statistical office or central bank. End-of-period values correspond to the rate observed in the last month of the reference period; average values correspond to the mean of the monthly rates within the reference period.

It excludes foreign content in re-exports and may differ from balance of payments data due to adjustments in timing, valuation and ownership recognition.

Imports in national accounts represent the value of goods and services acquired from the rest of the world, recorded on the basis of economic ownership rather than physical entry into the country. This measure includes both tangible goods and intangible services, as well as cases where goods are purchased from abroad without physically crossing the border, such as merchanting or goods processed abroad but owned domestically. It excludes goods merely in transit and may differ from balance of payments imports due to adjustments in timing, valuation, and ownership recognition.

Inflation is the percentage change in the Consumer Price Index (CPI) relative to the immediately preceding period of equal length, measuring the rate at which the general level of prices for goods and services purchased by households changes over time. A positive rate indicates a general increase in prices; a negative rate indicates deflation. The CPI basket, weighting methodology, and base year vary across countries and may be revised periodically by national statistical offices or central banks. End-of-period values correspond to the rate observed in the last month of the reference period against the previous last month of the previous reference period; average values correspond to the mean of the monthly rates within the reference period against the previous reference period.

Non-tradable GDP at constant prices is the value of gross domestic product generated by non-tradable sectors of the economy, such as construction, retail trade and most services, measured at constant prices of a fixed base year. The classification of non-tradable sectors may vary across countries. Tradable and non-tradable GDP shares are computed as a percentage of total GDP at constant prices. Since sectoral aggregates are constructed from value added while total GDP is measured at market prices, the two do not necessarily coincide. To ensure consistency, any discrepancy is allocated proportionally between tradable and non-tradable components based on their relative shares, so that their sum equals total GDP.
Source: Internal calculations based on INDEC - Argentina

Definition: Public external debt is the stock of outstanding debt owed by the public sector of a country to nonresidents. It includes the obligations of all entities that report under public external debt statistics, such as the central government, local governments and public enterprises. These obligations may take the form of loans, bonds or other financial liabilities denominated in foreign or domestic currency, provided the creditors are abroad. This indicator reflects the external borrowing of the public sector and its exposure to foreign financial risks. The definition may vary by country.

It typically covers savings deposits, small time deposits and foreign currency deposits held by residents.

Definition: The Real Exchange Rate (RER) bilateral vis-à-vis the US dollar is an index that measures the relative price of domestic goods and services compared to those of the United States. It is calculated by adjusting the nominal exchange rate with the ratio of the domestic Consumer Price Index (CPI) to the U.S. CPI.

Definition: Tradable GDP at constant prices is the value of gross domestic product generated by tradable sectors of the economy, such as manufacturing, mining and agriculture, measured at constant prices of a fixed base year. The classification of tradable sectors may vary across countries. Tradable and non-tradable GDP shares are computed as a percentage of total GDP at constant prices. Since sectoral aggregates are constructed from value added while total GDP is measured at market prices, the two do not necessarily coincide. To ensure consistency, any discrepancy is allocated proportionally between tradable and non-tradable components based on their relative shares, so that their sum equals total GDP.
Source: Internal calculations based on INDEC - Argentina
